title: What Is LORAN-A? — Definition
body:
Finding the way before GPS: the magnetic compass, astrolabe and quadrant, cross-staff and backstaff, sextant and octant, chip log and lead line, marine chronometer, LORAN/Decca/Omega radio systems, and the Transit satellites that preceded GPS.

In the context of this database, the LORAN-A is presented as one navigation record among the navigation history family. 1942's pulses: the hyperbolic — WWII's navigation.

title: Origins and History of LORAN-A
body:
The LORAN-A belongs to the 1942–1980s era and traces to MIT Rad Lab.

Chinese lodestone compasses (11th c.) reached the Mediterranean by the 1200s; dead reckoning and latitude sailing crossed oceans. The astrolabe and quadrant measured star altitudes; the cross-staff (1500s) and Davis backstaff improved it. Hadley and Godfrey's octant (1731) and the sextant (1757) gave arc-minute precision; Harrison's chronometer gave longitude. The 20th century electrified it: radio direction finding, LORAN (WWII), Decca, Omega, then Transit satellites (1960s) — the first satellite navigation, Doppler-based, for Polaris submarines. GPS (first satellite 1978, full 1995) ended the era.

Within that longer story, LORAN-A: The 1942 operational; the 1980s' sunset. The LORAN is the pulse's fix.

title: How LORAN-A Works
body:
Celestial navigation measures a body's altitude above the horizon with a sextant; with the exact time (chronometer) and the Nautical Almanac, sight reduction yields a line of position — two or three give a fix. Dead reckoning advances position by course and speed (chip log, then taffrail log). Radio systems (LORAN) timed pulses from synchronized stations: time differences are hyperbolic lines of position. Transit satellites' Doppler shift gave a fix to submarines that briefly raised an antenna.

Applied to the LORAN-A (1942–1980s, MIT Rad Lab): The LORAN is the pulse's fix.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of LORAN-A — Components
body:
Every LORAN-A is an assembly of the navigation history family's standard parts:

• Sextant frame — Arc, mirrors, shades; measures to 0.1 arc-minute.
• Index & horizon mirrors — Bring the body down to the horizon.
• Telescope / sight tube — Magnifies the contact.
• Micrometer drum — Fine altitude reading.
• Chronometer — GMT to the second; longitude's key.
• Nautical almanac — Daily celestial positions; sight-reduction tables.
• Compass & binnacle — Magnetic direction with deviation correction.
• Chip log / taffrail log — Speed through water measurement.
• Lead line — Depth sounding with marked line; 'by the mark'.
• LORAN receiver — Pulse timing to hyperbolic fix.

When examining a surviving LORAN-A, identify these parts in order: Sextant frame, Index & horizon mirrors, Telescope / sight tube, Micrometer drum, Chronometer, Nautical almanac.

title: Navigation History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of navigation history:

• latitude by noon sight — Sun's meridian altitude gives latitude directly.
• longitude problem — Solved by Harrison's chronometer; time = east-west.
• sight reduction — Math turning sextant altitude into a position line.
• intercept — Difference between observed and computed altitude.
• dead reckoning — Advancing position by course/speed; 'deduced reckoning'.
• great circle — Shortest path on a sphere; vs rhumb line.
• deviation / variation — Compass errors: shipboard vs magnetic-vs-true.
• LORAN — Long Range Navigation; hyperbolic pulse system.
• Transit — First satnav; Doppler fixes for submarines.
• fix — Position from crossing lines of position.
• knot — Nautical mile per hour; from the chip log's knots.
• fathom — Six feet; the lead line's unit.

title: LORAN-A in Culture
body:
'By the mark twain' (two fathoms) named Mark Twain. The sextant is the mariner's slide rule — still taught, still raced in celestial rallies. LORAN chains dotted Cold War coasts; 'shooting the sun' at noon is a ritual older than nations. GPS made it invisible; the skills became sport.

The LORAN-A carries that cultural charge directly: The LORAN is the pulse's fix.

title: Collecting and Preserving LORAN-A
body:
Brass sextants (Heath, Hughes, Tamaya) hold value — check mirrors and arc silvering. Octants are rarer and dearer. Chronometers need servicing; buy with box and gimbals. Lead lines and taffrail logs are affordable nautical décor with real history.

For the LORAN-A specifically: 1942's pulses: the hyperbolic — WWII's navigation.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working LORAN-A with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: LORAN-A Restoration Guide
body:
Clean mirrors with lens tissue only; resilver arcs professionally. Chronometers: full service, keep wound. Check sextant for arc error with the sun (shades!). Store brass oiled in dry conditions.

Restoration order for a LORAN-A: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical navigation record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: LORAN-A — Noon-sight latitude + dead reckoning (Runnable Python)
body:
Computes latitude from a meridian sun sight and advances a dead-reckoning position — the daily math of the celestial navigator.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the LORAN-A so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Celestial noon sight + dead reckoning (public-domain navigation math)
def latitude_noon(sun_alt_deg, declination_deg, sun_bearing):
    # lat = 90 - Ho + dec (sign by hemisphere); simplified
    lat = 90 - sun_alt_deg + (declination_deg if sun_bearing == "S" else -declination_deg)
    return lat

print(f"noon sight: Ho=62deg30', dec=+20deg, sun to S -> lat = "
      f"{latitude_noon(62.5, 20.0, 'S'):.2f} deg")

import math
def dr(lat_deg, lon_deg, course_deg, speed_kn, hours):
    # plane sailing approximation
    d = speed_kn * hours
    c = math.radians(course_deg)
    dlat = d * math.cos(c) / 60
    dep = d * math.sin(c)
    dlon = dep / (60 * math.cos(math.radians(lat_deg)))
    return lat_deg + dlat, lon_deg + dlon

lat, lon = dr(40.0, -70.0, 90, 8, 6)
print(f"DR after 6h at 8kt due east from 40N 70W: {lat:.2f}N, {abs(lon):.2f}W")
